newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Eyeing China, Taiwan is boosting soyoil capacity.
newsitem.headline: Eyeing China, Taiwan is boosting soyoil capacity.

text.p: Taiwan soybean crushers eager to tap China's huge market will more than double their soyoil capacity by 1999, local traders said on Monday.
"Taiwan soyoil makers are expanding to catch China's booming market," a soybean buyer said. "Soy oil consumption by mainland Chinese will increase as their incomes rise."

Four major Taiwan soybean crushing groups are expanding capacity rapidly and traders say this will push the island's soyoil production capacity to 660,000 tonnes a year in 1999 from 320,000 tonnes now, a 106 percent increase.
Taiwan is expected to export about 50,000 tonnes of soyoil in 1996 -- about 35,000 tonnes of it to China -- but exports could jump to 250,000 tonnes a year by 1998.

Traders expect that Taiwan's longtime diplomatic rival will become the island's main market if direct shipping links across the Taiwan strait can be established, though such links remain prohibited by Taiwan.
"If we could use handy-size ships to transport soyoil to China, exports to China would jump," a soyoil producer said.
A handy-size vessel carries about 30,000 tonnes.

Traders cautioned that no one can predict when direct links with China can begin, although Taipei and Beijing have expressed support in principle for the concept and have offered their own proposals for how it would work.
"We don't know if direct links with China will ever become a reality, but we must start to position now," the soyoil producer said.
Taiwan has banned direct transport, communications and other official links with communist China since the Chinese civil war split them in 1949.
Beijing regards Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province and has been turning up pressure on the island to accept communist rule and reunify with the mainland.
Taiwan wholesale soyoil prices on Monday ranged from T$18 to T$21 per kg.
Taiwan's Central Union plans to build a silo and crushing plant in the port of Taichung in early 1998 to produce 140,000 to 160,000 tonnes of soyoil a year, traders said.
Central Union is a T$1 billion (US$36.4 million) joint venture of Chia Hsin, Formosa Oilseeds, Fwu Sou Grain and Tay Shan, traders said.
The union's members now produce about 140,000 tonnes soyoil a year, but traders said most of their factories are antiquated and would be closed once the joint venture plant is operating.
Sources said Taiwan's Ttet Union will increase its soybean crushing capacity to about 160,000 tonnes by 1998 from 94,000 tonnes soyoil in 1996.
Taiwan's Hui Shung Group will expand its soyoil production to 120,000 tonnes a year by opening a new 60,000 tonnes-a-year plant in the Philippines in 1998, a group official said.
Another group, Ta-Jung, will expand its capacity to about 140,000 tonnes of soyoil a year by 1999 from 22,000 tonnes in 1996, traders estimated.
